title: Beyond Evidence-Informed Practices
author: solinthewild
summary: Sol in the Wild maps Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction onto the Instructional Hierarchy framework, arguing that the 'evidence-informed practice' conversation in education has produced a list of things to do but not a theory of when each thing is appropriate. The Instructional Hierarchy identifies four stages of skill development -- acquisition (introducing a new skill), fluency (developing speed and ease), generalization (applying the skill to new contexts), and adaptation (modifying the skill to handle novel problems) -- and argues that different instructional practices are effective at different stages. Rosenshine's Principles, the piece argues, are largely acquisition and fluency strategies: they excel at introducing new material and building automaticity, but they do not map onto generalization and adaptation, which require different pedagogical moves (open-ended tasks, low-scaffolding problem-solving, transfer activities). The piece is a practical curriculum planning tool: it gives teachers a framework for asking not just 'what is evidence-based?' but 'what is evidence-based for where this student is in the learning progression?'
points: * The Instructional Hierarchy provides a four-stage model of skill development (acquisition, fluency, generalization, adaptation) that specifies not just what to teach but what instructional moves are appropriate at each stage. * Rosenshine's Principles are primarily acquisition and fluency strategies: they are highly effective for introducing new material and building automaticity but are not mapped to the generalization and adaptation stages, where different approaches are needed. * The 'evidence-based practice' conversation often produces a list of universally recommended strategies without specifying the learning stage where each strategy has the supporting evidence -- a gap the Instructional Hierarchy fills. * Generalization and adaptation require instructional moves that are the near-opposite of acquisition moves: lower scaffolding, open-ended tasks, novel problem contexts, and deliberate transfer practice rather than guided instruction. * The framework is a curriculum planning tool: it allows teachers to ask 'where is this student in the hierarchy for this skill?' and select instructional approaches matched to that stage rather than applying the same strategies across all stages.
quotes: We have been very good at generating lists of evidence-based practices. We have been less good at specifying when each practice is evidence-based for. Rosenshine's Principles are excellent. They are also, largely, acquisition and fluency practices. Using them with students who are at the generalization stage is not wrong exactly -- it is suboptimal in a way that the evidence won't tell you.

The Instructional Hierarchy is not a replacement for Rosenshine. It is a map that tells you where Rosenshine fits. The explicit instruction, the guided practice, the high success rate -- these are acquisition moves. They get the skill into the student. But getting the skill in is not the same as making the skill usable in a new context.

Generalization is the hardest stage to teach because the instructional instincts that worked at acquisition actively interfere with it. The student who learned to identify the main idea with teacher support needs to identify the main idea without teacher support, in an unfamiliar text, on a topic they haven't studied. Providing the same scaffolds at this stage is not helpful. It is the barrier.

Adaptation is the stage almost no curriculum reaches. This is where the student doesn't just apply a skill -- they modify it for a novel problem. The essay writer who encounters a text type they've never seen before and adapts their analytical approach. The mathematician who applies a known procedure to a structurally new kind of problem. Teaching for adaptation requires radical departure from instruction and radical trust in the learner.

The question I want every teacher to be able to answer for every skill they teach is: where are my students in the hierarchy? Not as a general claim about the class -- for each student, for this skill, right now. That question changes lesson planning, it changes feedback, and it changes what counts as progress.
